title: Protecting the Bargain

actors.name: Visiting criminals
actors.role: Described as participants in the arrangement

actors.name: People harmed outside the city
actors.role: Excluded from the bargain; analytical perspective

aims: Refuge and predictable access offered reasons to cooperate; private motives and exact compliance remain an interpretation.
mechanism: An intermediary could make access selective and repeated dealings more predictable. A criminal hoping to return had a reason to respect local limits; an official receiving money had a reason to preserve a paying relationship. A conspicuous local crime threatened the benefits others expected from the arrangement. The boundary also shifted costs. Keeping an offense outside Saint Paul could serve participants' interests without making anyone beyond the city safer. The excluded parties matter: victims elsewhere had not agreed to finance local calm with their own exposure to violence. This is a model of incentives, not proof that the arrangement eliminated local crime or worked uniformly. Later kidnappings will show how an immediate opportunity could conflict with maintaining refuge.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: People harmed by crimes and excluded from protection.
observedResponse: MNHS describes both efforts to preserve the arrangement and changes in its leadership. No compliance rate is established.
evidentiaryLimit: Succession is not proof of a personal meeting between Griffin and Hogan.

title: Influencing the Decision

actors.name: Leon Gleckman
actors.role: Defendant in tax and contempt proceedings

actors.name: Bernard Fuchs
actors.role: Juror described in the contempt opinion

actors.name: Investigators and prosecutors
actors.role: Developed the financial and contempt cases

aims: An effort to influence jurors is established in the contempt case. Prosecutors separately sought to prove taxable income.
mechanism: There were two contests here: proving the tax case and influencing the people who would decide it. The contempt findings document an attempt to affect that second contest. Fuchs received benefits; Gleckman sought favorable intervention. Credit could become a means of obligation, while the transactions and testimony supplied evidence against the effort. It is tempting to make a conviction explain an entire city's politics. Resist that shortcut. These proceedings support particular findings about Gleckman. They do not prove every story told about him, every meeting imagined inside the hotel, or complicity by every person who knew him.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: The integrity of jury deliberation and equal treatment before the law.
observedResponse: The tax and contempt opinions record distinct proceedings, a partial acquittal, and convictions upheld on appeal. A mistrial alone does not establish a single holdout juror.
evidentiaryLimit: The findings concern Gleckman. Do not assign Fuchs an unverified legal outcome.

title: Making a Place Desirable

actors.name: Patrons
actors.role: Audience for the venue; individual guest identities not established

aims: An unusual setting could attract paying customers. This is an interpretation of the venue’s presentation, not measured profit or proof of criminal protection.
mechanism: Turning an unusual physical space into an attraction could distinguish a business competing for customers. The supported analysis concerns entertainment and presentation. The evidence examined does not establish a criminal protection arrangement at Castle Royal. Later memory layer, explicitly outside the 1930s: Famous names can make a place's story more compelling. That creates an incentive worth examining, but it does not prove anyone knowingly invented a claim. Comparing the age and type of evidence is more useful than letting atmosphere decide the question.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: Readers who could mistake atmosphere for evidence.
observedResponse: A 1933 business announcement and Brick’s account support venue history. Later guest recollections remain contested.
evidentiaryLimit: Disputed guest stories remain disputed; no origin date or intentional invention is established.

title: Taking a Payoff, Spreading the Cost
aims: Captors demanded a large immediate payment; the family faced an urgent threat to Hamm’s life.
mechanism: A major ransom offered an immediate gain to its captors. The costs could extend beyond them: a victim and family suffered directly, while scrutiny could threaten other people depending on refuge. This is the conflict between an individual opportunity and a shared arrangement. Payment and investigation also operated on different time horizons. A family's urgent concern was a person's return; investigators could continue seeking evidence afterward. Those interests should not be presented as a simple contest between courage and weakness. Hamm's kidnapping occurred before national repeal that December. A June event cannot be explained as the consequence of a later date.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: Hamm and his family, with wider scrutiny affecting the refuge system.
observedResponse: Ransom was paid and Hamm was released alive. The FBI retrospective describes subsequent fingerprint identification.
evidentiaryLimit: Agency retrospective; neither a laboratory report examined here nor a claim of global forensic priority.

title: Controlling the Response

actors.name: Local and federal authorities
actors.role: Received notification according to the summary

aims: The communications tried to secure payment and discourage police involvement. That aim did not dictate the family’s response.
mechanism: The bank-robbery comparison reveals an alleged attempt to change the target of extraction: from institutional cash to the amount relatives and associates could be compelled to produce. The ransom pressure then tried to control the response as well as the payment. The limits are just as revealing as the strategy. Demanding secrecy did not guarantee secrecy. Expecting a higher payoff did not guarantee a stable refuge afterward. Participants could seek short-term advantage without controlling the investigation their actions produced. Bremer and Magee were operating under coercion. Explaining their constrained choices must never turn the tour into a puzzle about how a victim should have outsmarted a captor.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: Bremer and people pressured to arrange his return.
observedResponse: The summary reports authorities were notified despite the captors’ threats. Bremer was later released.
evidentiaryLimit: An attributed investigative reconstruction cannot supply every participant’s private reasoning.

title: The Limits of a Safe Place

actors.name: Dillinger and Frechette
actors.role: Used an alias at Lincoln Court in the agency account

aims: An alias could help conceal identity. The record does not establish a prior wound to heal or a paid guarantee for this apartment.
mechanism: An alias works only while other people accept or cannot penetrate it. A local accommodation is valuable only to the extent that relevant officials honor it—and only within the reach of that accommodation. Another authority, a manager's observation, or an associate's exposure can change the situation. The broader lesson is conditional security. People pursuing refuge could not control every observer or investigating body. The record shows reporting and intervention; it does not tell us the manager's private motive, establish a paid betrayal, or justify inventing an informer reward. Frechette belongs in this account as a named person with her own subsequent legal outcome. Association with Dillinger does not itself establish participation in his bank robberies.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: Residents, staff, and officers exposed to armed confrontation.
observedResponse: The manager’s report preceded surveillance and the March 31 confrontation; Dillinger escaped wounded in the agency account.
evidentiaryLimit: No checked floor plan, exact time of confrontation, or exhaustive witness comparison.

title: Changing Who Can Apply Pressure
aims: Prosecution addressed individual conduct; appointment rules could reduce dependence on political favor.
mechanism: Reform could target the conditions sustaining protection: expose relationships, prosecute provable conduct, and change how officials acquired and retained office. These approaches addressed different weaknesses. Evidence could damage secrecy; job protections could reduce one route for political pressure. The sources also deserve the questions asked of their subjects. A police history may emphasize professional reform; an agency history may emphasize investigative success. Those perspectives do not invalidate their evidence, but they cannot establish the whole story by themselves. The end of this route is therefore a change in the conditions of power, supported by particular outcomes. It is not proof that corruption disappeared or that all harms were repaired.
expectedBenefit: The expected advantage is an interpretation described above, not proof of success or private intent.
bearingCosts: People affected by corruption, and defendants subject to specific adjudicated outcomes.
observedResponse: The cited accounts record legal outcomes and formal reform, without establishing an end to all corruption.
evidentiaryLimit: Reform changed formal rules; it does not establish that all corruption disappeared.
